summary: Abram challenges Terah's idols, later burns their shrine, and leaves Ur after Haran dies in the fire. In Haran he rejects star-based prediction, prays for direction, receives a call to Canaan, and is taught the language of the book's primeval records before Terah blesses his departure.
whyItMatters: Abram's move is presented as a turn from inherited worship and omen reading toward direct dependence on God, setting up the land and family promises.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Abram's household in Ur and then Haran, before his journey to Canaan.
context.literaryForm: Expanded ancestral narrative with anti-idol speech, prayer, divine call, and language explanation.

before.text: Abram has separated from his father’s idols and gained notice by protecting sowing from ravens.

here.text: He challenges the idols, rejects omen reading, receives a divine call, and prepares to leave his family’s place.

after.text: Abram enters Canaan with Sarai and Lot, builds altars, and hears the first land promise there.

outline.heading: Abram confronts Terah’s idols
outline.note: Terah fears the response of the surrounding community.

outline.heading: Family and the fire at Ur
outline.note: Marriages are listed, Abram burns the shrine, and Haran dies.

outline.heading: Abram rejects star prediction and prays
outline.note: He entrusts rain, the future, and his route to God.

outline.heading: Call, promise, and restored language
outline.note: God commands departure and the angel teaches Abram to read ancestral books.

outline.heading: Terah blesses the journey
outline.note: Abram announces his plan and receives a father’s farewell.

keyVerses.text: And a word came into his heart and he said: All the signs of the stars, and the signs of the moon and of the sun are all in the hand of the Lord. Why do I search (them) out?
keyVerses.why: Abram turns from consulting celestial signs to the Lord who governs them.

keyVerses.text: And he made an end of speaking and praying, and behold the word of the Lord was sent to him through me, saying: 'Get thee up from thy country, and from thy kindred and from the house of thy father unto a land which I will show thee, and I shall make thee a great and numerous nation.
keyVerses.why: The call to leave country and kin begins the journey that structures the next chapters.

questions.question: What is Abram’s objection to Terah’s idols?
questions.answer: He says they are human-made, lifeless forms that cannot give help, while God gives rain and life. His case is about worship and dependence, not about whether crafted objects can have artistic value.

questions.question: Why does Terah agree yet tell Abram to stay silent?
questions.answer: Terah says he knows Abram’s criticism is true but fears the worshippers will kill him if he speaks openly. The story leaves Terah in a compromised position rather than describing him as simply convinced or simply unaware.

questions.question: What does the chapter say happened when Abram burned the idol house?
questions.answer: He sets it on fire secretly at night, and Haran dies while trying to rescue the images. The text reports that sequence but does not say Abram intended Haran’s death; it also does not present arson here as a general instruction for readers.

questions.question: What are the “signs of the stars” Abram stops consulting?
questions.answer: Abram watches the sky to judge what the year’s rains will be like, then questions why he is searching these signs. His prayer shifts attention to the Lord who can give or withhold rain.

questions.question: What is promised when Abram is told to leave?
questions.answer: The speech promises a land to be shown, a numerous nation, blessing, and a continuing relationship with his descendants. The promise comes after Abram asks for a path forward, rather than after he has already reached Canaan.

questions.question: Does “Hebrew in the tongue of the creation” prove the historical language of Adam?
questions.answer: The angel makes that claim inside Jubilees’ story and says Abram can study ancestral books written in Hebrew. It is a literary assertion about sacred language in this work, not independent evidence of what prehistoric people spoke.

questions.question: How does Terah respond to Abram’s plan to visit Canaan?
questions.answer: Terah blesses his route, asks him to bring Lot, and says he might later join if Abram finds a suitable land. This farewell is more supportive than his earlier fearful response to the criticism of idols.

glossary.def: Human-made objects that Abram says cannot give life or help and should not receive worship.
The people and region associated in this account with Abram’s home at Ur and with omen reading.
